core: UPDATE changes the values stored in existing rows of a table; it does not add rows (INSERT) or remove them (DELETE)
Basic shape: UPDATE table_name SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, ... WHERE condition
SET holds the assignments: column name on the left of the equals sign, new value on the right; several columns can be set at once
The WHERE clause specifies which rows are updated; omitting WHERE updates all rows in the table
The database may reject an UPDATE that violates a constraint (e.g., NOT NULL, uniqueness, foreign key) by raising an error
UPDATE is a write operation: the change is permanent and the old values are gone once the statement runs
supporting: A WHERE condition that matches no rows is not an error; the UPDATE simply affects zero rows
Only rows for which the WHERE condition evaluates to true are updated (PostgreSQL)
Text values are written in single quotes and numbers bare in SET assignments, as elsewhere in SQL
Safe practice: run a SELECT with the same WHERE clause before an UPDATE to see which rows will change, and again afterward to confirm
outOfScope: WHERE condition operators and syntax in depth (sibling topic: where)
Constraint definitions and table design (sibling topics: primary-keys, foreign-keys, data-integrity)
Transactions and rollback of updates (sibling topic: transactions)

claims.claim: The UPDATE statement modifies the values stored in existing rows of a table: it changes the values of the specified columns in the rows that satisfy the condition, rather than adding or removing rows.
The basic shape of an update is UPDATE table_name SET column1 = value1, column2 = value2, ... WHERE condition; the WHERE clause specifies which records should be updated.
If the UPDATE statement has no WHERE clause, all rows in the table are modified; W3Schools warns explicitly that omitting the WHERE clause updates ALL records.
Only rows for which the WHERE condition evaluates to true are updated; it is not an error if the condition matches no rows, in which case the UPDATE affects zero rows.
The SET clause lists assignments with a column name to the left of the equals sign and a new value (an expression) to the right; several columns can be assigned in one UPDATE statement.

Constraints are rules on the data; if a user attempts to store data that would violate a constraint, an error is raised, so the database may reject an UPDATE that breaks a rule such as NOT NULL, uniqueness, or a foreign key.
UPDATE is a write operation: it permanently changes the stored values in the table, in contrast to SELECT, which only reads data back.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether an UPDATE without a WHERE clause is an error
positions: Some learners assume the database will refuse an UPDATE that has no WHERE clause
Standard SQL treats it as valid: without WHERE, all rows in the table are modified; W3Schools and SQLite both state this explicitly
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson teaches that omitting WHERE is valid SQL that updates every row — the classic danger — and demonstrates it with an original example (UPDATE products SET stock = 0;) executed against SQLite, which confirmed all five rows changed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What happens when an UPDATE would violate a constraint
positions: A learner might expect the database to store the bad value anyway
PostgreSQL documents that attempting to store data that violates a constraint raises an error, so the update fails instead
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson teaches that the database rejects constraint-breaking updates with an error; verified against SQLite, which refused UPDATE products SET name = NULL (NOT NULL constraint) and a duplicate product_id (UNIQUE constraint).

sourceRecords.notes: Official documentation (Tier A per subject source-map). Read live on 2026-08-21.
